finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id deletes the report even when the authorization check fails, because authorize() is called without await, so its 403 rejection never reaches the handler's control flow.
finding.source: Any HTTP DELETE request to /reports/:id from a caller whose grants lack "delete" on that report, including a request with no session user (req.user undefined).
finding.sink: server.js:21 db.reports.remove(report.id) runs unconditionally, and server.js:22 returns 204 to the attacker.

trace.note: req.user is copied from req.session.user with no check that it is set.
DELETE handler starts; the report is loaded by attacker-supplied id.
authorize(req.user,"delete",report) is called without await or return. The async function runs to its first await (db.grants) and returns a pending promise to the handler, which ignores it.
Inside authorize, db.grants(user.id, resource.id) is awaited. If req.user is undefined, user.id throws here and the rejection is also unobserved.
If the grants array does not include "delete", the check fails.
The 403 error is thrown, which only rejects the promise that nothing awaits. It cannot stop the handler.
The handler continues and removes the report. The deletion is not gated on the authorization result.
The handler responds 204 No Content, so the caller sees success.

finding.guards_checked: Checked: authorize() is declared async and throws, but the call site at line 20 does not await or return it, so the throw cannot stop execution. No try/catch around the call. No route-level or app-level authorization middleware in this file. The PUT handler at line 27 does use await, so the guard is applied only to DELETE. No ownership check beyond the grants lookup. Confidence high for the control-flow defect; exploitability depends on db.grants returning a list without "delete" for the caller, which is the normal case for non-owners.

verdict.guard_found: none. authorize() (server.js:9-16) signals failure only by throwing and returns no bool. The call at server.js:20 is a bare statement with no await, return, or try/catch. The only route-level code is the middleware at server.js:4-7, which does no authorization. The PUT handler at server.js:27 awaits authorize, so the guard is applied to DELETE only.
verdict.reason: At server.js:20 authorize() is called without await, so its rejection at server.js:14 cannot stop the handler, and server.js:21 deletes the report and server.js:22 returns 204 regardless. Any authenticated non-owner whose grants lack "delete" can trigger this; the one caveat is that server.js:5 reads req.session, which this file never sets up, so the route is only reachable if session middleware is mounted elsewhere.

finding.claim: A forbidden or malformed PUT/DELETE request produces an unhandled promise rejection. On Node 15+ with default settings this terminates the whole process, and the client gets no response.
finding.source: Any authenticated user without "write" (or "delete") grant on a report, or any anonymous request whose req.user is undefined, or any request for a nonexistent report id. The attacker controls the :id path parameter and the session.
finding.sink: Process availability: the rejected promise from the async route handler at server.js:27 (and server.js:20 for DELETE) is unhandled.

trace.note: PUT handler is an async arrow function with no try/catch and no .catch.
db.reports.get(req.params.id) with a nonexistent id yields null or undefined.
await authorize(...) throws err.status=403 when grants are missing. If report is null, resource.id at server.js:10 throws a TypeError instead.
The 403 is never sent to the client. Express 4 does not forward rejections from async handlers to error middleware, so the rejection goes to the process-level unhandledRejection path.
app.listen(3003) runs in the same process, so a crash takes down service for all users. The same unhandled-rejection path is reachable from DELETE at server.js:20 (see F1).

finding.guards_checked: Checked: no try/catch in either route, no app.use error handler, no process.on('unhandledRejection') handler in this file. The err.status = 403 is set but nothing reads it. The Express version is not pinned in this directory (no package.json), so the Express 4 assumption is unverified; under Express 5, async rejections are forwarded to error middleware and this crash would not occur, though the 403 would still be a 500 or ignored unless an error handler maps it. Node 15+ default unhandled-rejection behavior is assumed (see the JavaScript footguns guide, section 7.3).

verdict.guard_found: none. server.js has no try/catch around the PUT (25-30) or DELETE (18-23) handlers, no app.use error middleware, and no process.on('unhandledRejection') handler. The only other control is authorize() (9-16), which throws rather than returning a bool, and its throw is not caught by either route. The 403 is set on err.status (13) but nothing reads it.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: authorize() throws at server.js:13-14, the PUT handler at server.js:25-27 has no catch, and the same unhandled path applies to the un-awaited authorize() at server.js:20. Whether that rejection crashes the process depends on the Express major version, which is not pinned in this directory (only server.js exists), and Express 5 forwards async rejections to error middleware instead of crashing, so the crash cannot be confirmed from the code available. The attacker reachability (any authenticated user without a write grant, or a nonexistent :id via server.js:26) is accurate.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id passes the entire request body to db.reports.update, so any writable field of the report, including ownership or access-control fields if they are stored on the record, can be set by a caller who only has "write" on that report.
finding.source: req.body from express.json() at server.js:3. The caller controls every key and value in the JSON object, subject only to a "write" grant on the report.
finding.sink: server.js:28 db.reports.update(report.id, req.body), an unfiltered write of attacker-controlled fields to the report record.

trace.note: express.json() parses the full request body with no field allowlist.
authorize(req.user,"write",report) gates the request on a per-report write grant only.
db.reports.update(report.id, req.body) writes the whole body. Keys such as owner, ownerId, grants, acl, or id are not removed.

finding.guards_checked: Checked: the PUT does await authorize at line 27, so a "write" grant is required. No schema, field allowlist, or pick/omit step exists in this file. The db module is not in the directory, so the record's fields and whether update() ignores unknown keys are unverified. If the report record holds only content fields, this is a lower-severity over-broad write rather than privilege escalation. Confidence medium pending the db schema.

verdict.guard_found: server.js:27 `await authorize(req.user, "write", report)` is effective: authorize (server.js:9-16) throws a 403 when the "write" grant is missing, so only callers with a write grant on that report reach the update. No field allowlist, schema validation, or pick/omit exists between server.js:3 and server.js:28.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: server.js:3 parses the full body, the write-grant check at server.js:27 is effective, and server.js:28 passes all of req.body to db.reports.update; whether this is privilege escalation or only an over-broad write depends on the report schema in the db module, which is not in the directory, so I cannot tell whether owner or ACL fields live on the record (db.grants at server.js:10 is a separate lookup, which suggests grants are not stored on the record).
